newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil still free of genetically-modified soybeans.
newsitem.headline: Brazil still free of genetically-modified soybeans.

text.p: Brazil is still a genetically modified soybean-free nation but moves are underway to begin production of the headline-grabbing cereal.

Test production may even take place in Brazil this crop year if given the go-ahead by a special committee of the Science and Technology Ministry, said a representative of the company which developed the soybean.
"We are expecting to hear by the end of this year from the committee," said Geraldo Berger of chemical firm Monsanto.
"But this is a formality, it is almost 100 percent certain it will be approved," he added.

The next stage would be trial production in special areas designated by the committee. This could still go ahead this crop year even though planting is normally completed by the end of December, Berger said.
Only after the test period is over however would the company be able to begin selling seeds on a general basis to producers.
Genetically modified soybeans from the U.S have recently been the subject of protests by European environmentalists who argue that the beans are a hazardous experiment with nature.
For producers, the attraction is lower cost given the bean has been developed to be resistant to one type of weedkiller, therefore removing the need to buy a mixture of herbicides, Berger said.

Environmentalist groups in Europe have recently blockaded various European ports to highlight their protest and some food groups such as Unilever's unit in Germany have pledged not to use the beans, even though they consider them safe.
Berger did not believe that the recent protests would affect the decision of the Science ministry committee.
"What is happening in Europe is pure emotion and is not based on scientific evidence," Berger said.
Some one to two percent of U.S. soybean exports are now expected to contain modified beans.
Berger said that Monsanto was waiting for approval from the ministry committee before making any projections as to what could be future production of modified beans within Brazil.
According to independent consultants Safras e Mercado, Brazilian soybean production in 1996/97 should reach 26.38 million tonnes, of which 5.4 million tonnes will be exported.

The export figure is a sharp rise on forecast 1995/96 overseas sales of 3.6 million tonnes and is due to beans becoming a more attractive option than soymeal and soyoil following the scrapping of a state export tax ICMS in mid-September, according to Safras.

The current debate over genetically-modified beans should also increase demand for "old-style" Brazilian soybeans overseas, said the secretary-general of the Brazilian Vegetable Oil Industries Association.
"Out of the U.S. for example, there is no way of guaranteeing whether beans are genetically-modified or not, there is no way of separating them," said Fabio Trigueirinho.
Sales of modified soybean seeds in Brazil's neighbour and other major soybean producer, Argentina, have already begun but sowings for the 1996/97 harvest are expected to be minimal.
